items.what: Backups of the firm's data (clients, portal, settings, accounts, the document index, the Clio connection) and a test restore
steps: The installer registers a nightly backup (python tools/backup.py --out <folder on another disk> --keep 14, with a passphrase file for encryption). Keeping current shows the last backup's date and the last test restore's date from data/backup_log.json; a backup older than 2 days or a test restore older than 31 days makes the item due.

Once a month: python tools/restore.py <the newest backup> --check (unpacks to a temporary folder, opens every JSON file and database, compares every sha256 and the case count with the backup's manifest, deletes itself, records the date).

Once a quarter: restore one backup with --into a new empty folder on a spare disk and open a client's packet from it. Keep the passphrase, and the Clio and authenticator key files when the backup is not encrypted, apart from the backups. Keys kept in the server's environment (I485_TOTP_KEY, CLIO_TOKEN_KEY) are in no backup: a restore onto a new server needs a copy of them.
firm_steps: Confirm last night's backup ran: its date is shown under this line.

items.what: The restore drill: the latest backup restored into a scratch folder and compared, record by record, with the live install
items.due_note: Also at once when the last drill failed. The overnight run does it on the first night of every month, and again when it is overdue.
where: src/backups.py (drill: what it compares and how a difference that came after the backup is told from one that did not)
data/backup_log.json (the last drill's result: the line under Settings)
steps: The overnight run restores the latest backup into a scratch folder on the first night of the month (the backup's passphrase is the installer's file install/backup_passphrase.txt, or I485_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE, or the file I485_BACKUP_PASSPHRASE_FILE names, in the overnight run's environment), compares every file with the live install, removes the scratch folder and records the result.

By hand: python tools/restore_drill.py (it takes the newest backup from the log, or give one); it prints each difference with the record, the field and the two times, and exits 1 when the drill failed.

A difference the live install made after the backup is expected and only counted; a difference in a file the install has not changed since the backup is a failure. A failure means the newest backup and the install disagree: make a new backup, run the drill again, and if it fails again restore the backup into a spare folder (tools/restore.py --into) and compare by hand before trusting any backup.
The drill never writes into the live install. The result is the line under Settings, and the morning report says it on the morning after a drill.

If it says failed, or the item is due, an attorney can press Run it now. A drill that fails means the newest backup cannot be relied on: tell your IT today and keep the old backups.

items.what: The computer's own duties (the disk encrypted, the screen locked, a recent backup on another device, the system updated, the firewall on): read what the product found and confirm each with the IT person

where: Settings, This computer (the five lines and, under each, "How this was checked")
steps: Settings, This computer: each line is on, off (red) or not known (grey). The product reads and never sets: it changes nothing on the machine.

For each line that is off or not known, the line says what IT does (the setting's name, or the command, per operating system): BitLocker or LUKS on the data disk; a screen lock of 15 minutes or less; the backup folder on another disk or a network share; the operating system's updates installed within 35 days; the firewall switched on.

A line that stays 'not known' (a server with no desktop has no screen lock to read; a Linux firewall that only an administrator can list) is a duty IT confirms by hand and notes here; it is not a pass.
Mark the item checked when IT has confirmed every line, and keep the date of the last reading beside the confirmation.

items.what: The written security program and the papers that go with it (incident plan, data flow, subpoena policy, summary of how the product keeps client data, exit procedure): re-read against what the product does today
items.due_note: Also whenever the product changes how it signs people in, stores, sends or logs data, and after any incident.
where: docs/public/data_statement.md (the same statement, as the pack's export writes it with the provider's name)
items.source: 201 CMR 17.03(2)(h) and (i): monitor the program, and review the scope of the security measures at least annually or whenever there is a material change in business practices (text read 10/02/2026 at https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/201-CMR-17-03; the mass.gov page was not readable)

check.note: Read each document against the code and the hardening guide; every sentence about what the product does must still be true. The pack is a draft until the provider's and the firm's attorneys have read it.

steps: Read docs/security/security_program.md heading by heading against the code (sign-in, sessions, logs, uploads, messages) and the hardening guide; correct anything that changed.
Check that every 'not yet' in the product data statement is still true, and move anything built since to the 'does today' list.
Re-read the sources named in each document (201 CMR 17.00, G.L. c. 93H, Fla. Stat. 501.171, the Florida and Massachusetts bar opinions) and note any change.
Have the provider's attorney re-read the changed parts. Record the check here.

After the statement or the list of outside services changes, run python tools/public_pages.py --no-sample: docs/public/security.md and data_statement.md are made from them, and a test fails until they are made again.

items.what: The yearly incident drill: walk through the incident plan with a made-up case and check that the contact list, the clocks and the evidence steps work
items.source: 201 CMR 17.03(2)(j) (document responsive actions and review them after an incident; text read 10/02/2026 at https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/201-CMR-17-03); ABA Formal Opinion 483 (lawyers' duties after a breach; a web summary was read 10/02/2026, the ABA's own page not seen); Fla. Stat. 501.171(6) (10 days to the firm) and (4) (30 days to individuals), read 10/02/2026 at http://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0500-0599/0501/Sections/0501.171.html

check.note: Run the drill with a made-up incident, with the firm's contact there if it can come; keep the notes with the check

steps: Pick a made-up incident (for example a lost laptop that held an export, or a staff password found in a leak list).
Walk the plan: who decides, who tells the firm, in how many days, who tells whom after that. Time each step against the 10-day and 30-day clocks.
Check that every contact in the contact tree is a working address or number, and that the evidence steps can be done on a real copy.
Write down what did not work, fix the plan, and record the check here.

items.source: 201 CMR 17.03(2)(f) (oversee service providers; text read 10/02/2026 at https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/massachusetts/201-CMR-17-03); Florida Bar Ethics Opinion 12-3 (others should not be able to access the information, and the lawyer should look into the provider's security; https://www.floridabar.org/etopinions/etopinion-12-3/, read 10/02/2026); ABA Formal Opinion 512 (AI tools; a web summary only, the ABA's page was not readable)

Confirm the document reader and the translator still run only on the firm's own machine (their code makes no outside call).
For each service: still used, still the same provider, still receives only what the list says; check the provider's own terms and breach-notice promise.
Update the list and tell each firm in writing before a new service is switched on. Record the check here.

items.what: Known vulnerabilities in the Python packages the system ships (requirements.lock), checked with pip-audit; patch a critical one within 7 days
steps: pip install -r requirements-dev.txt, then bash tools/check_deps.sh (exit 0: none known; 1: some found, listed with their fixed versions).
For each finding: upgrade the package in a copy, run the whole unit and browser test suites, regenerate requirements.lock (pip freeze, keep its header) and release.
Run it before every release too, and note the date here.
items.firm_what: Security fixes for the software's building blocks: a monthly check for known weaknesses
firm_steps: Once a month, run the vulnerability check {provider} supplies with the software, on the machine that runs it.
If it finds anything, ask {provider} for the update that fixes it and install it as with any update (a copy first, then the firm's machine).
A weakness marked critical: install the fix within 7 days.

items.what: HTTPS in front of the review app and the client portal (Caddy or nginx): the certificate is current and nothing answers over plain HTTP from outside
where: the proxy's configuration on the server (docs/hardening.md has the reference Caddyfile and nginx files)
steps: Open both apps by their https:// names from a staff computer: the browser shows no certificate warning, and the certificate's expiry is more than 30 days away (Caddy renews on its own; nginx certificates are renewed by whoever issued them).
Open the http:// name: it is sent to https:// (or refused), never served.
The review app was started with --trusted-proxy (or --behind-tls-proxy) and the portal with PORTAL_TRUSTED_PROXY when they sit behind the proxy.
items.firm_what: The secure (HTTPS) connection in front of the review app and the client portal
firm_steps: Open the review app and the client portal from a staff computer: the browser shows a padlock and no warning.
Check the security certificate does not run out in the next 30 days; renew it before it does.
Try the address with http:// instead of https://: it must switch to https:// or refuse.

items.what: Disk encryption on the machine that holds data/ and clients/ (BitLocker on Windows, LUKS on Linux), and where its recovery key is kept
where: the server's disks, and every disk a backup is written to
steps: Windows: manage-bde -status shows Protection On for every drive holding data/ or clients/; Linux: lsblk -f shows crypto_LUKS under them.
The recovery key is in the firm's password manager or safe, not on the same machine; backup disks are encrypted too.
items.firm_what: Encryption of the disks that hold client files, and its recovery key
firm_steps: Confirm disk encryption is on for every disk that holds client files or their backups (BitLocker on Windows, LUKS on Linux).
Confirm the recovery key is kept somewhere safe away from the machine (the firm's password manager or safe), and who can reach it.

items.what: Which network can reach each app: the review app only from the office network or the VPN, never the internet; the portal only through its HTTPS proxy
where: the firewall and router of the office, and the server's own firewall
steps: From outside the office (a phone off the office Wi-Fi), the review app's address must not answer; the portal answers only on https (443).
On the server, the apps' own ports (8485 review, 8600 portal) listen on 127.0.0.1 or the office network only, never on an address the router forwards from the internet.
items.firm_what: Who can reach the review app: the office and the firm's VPN only
firm_steps: From a phone that is not on the office Wi-Fi, try to open the review app: it must not open.
Confirm the client portal opens only with https:// and the review app only from the office or the firm's VPN.

items.what: Who has a review app account and which role; leavers turned off the same day; who may run the apps and read the server's folders
where: the staff accounts (src/review/users.py list), review_users_access.jsonl and review_views.jsonl beside them
steps: python src/review/users.py list: every account is a current staff member with the right role; disable anyone who left (it ends their sessions at once).
Only the service account that runs the apps, and named IT staff, can log on to the server or read data/ and clients/.
Skim the sign-in log for failures from unknown addresses and the view log for cases opened by someone not working on them.
Each restricted case (src/restricted.py; access.json in the case folder): the staff named on it still work it, and the view log's rows marked restricted show only them and the attorneys.
items.firm_what: Who can sign in to the review app, and who can reach the machine that runs it
firm_steps: With your IT, go through the list of staff accounts: everyone on it still works here and has the right role (paralegal or attorney).
Anyone who leaves: their account is turned off the same day.
Only the firm's IT staff can sign in to the machine that runs the apps.
Look at who viewed sensitive cases (the case's Decision log, Who viewed this) for anyone who should not have.
Go through the restricted cases (VAWA, T, U, asylum, and any an attorney restricted): everyone named on each still works on it; take off anyone who does not.

items.what: The provider's support sessions: each one asked for, as short as it needed, plain only when it had to be, and ended
where: Settings, Let support in (the current session and the last ten; src/support.py)
review_users.json (users.<email>.support and support_history), review_users_access.jsonl (support_let_in, support_request, support_ended) and the event ledger (kind support)
steps: Settings, Let support in: every session in the last ten was asked for by the firm, by an attorney who can say why.
Each lasted no longer than the problem needed (the hours chosen, and when it ended: by itself or by whom).
Each plain session (client values shown) had a reason the attorney can name; masked is the default.

Skim the support rows of the event ledger (kind support) or the access log (support_request) for a session: the pages support opened match the problem it was let in for, and no session is open that nobody remembers.
Nothing outside the product: no copy of the folders and no server login was given to the provider without the firm's written consent.
items.firm_what: The provider's support sessions: who let support in, for how long, and whether client values were shown
firm_steps: Open Settings, Let support in: look at the session open now, if any, and the last ten.
For each one: the firm asked for it, it lasted no longer than needed, and it ended (by itself or by an attorney).
For each session where client values were shown: the attorney who allowed it can say why.
If a session looks wrong, ask {provider} what their support person looked at: every page they opened is in the firm's record under their name.

items.what: The firm-wide document index behind Search: it is kept in one file next to the client folders, rebuilt for any case whose documents changed each night, and made again from scratch if the file is damaged or missing
steps: Search for a word from a document scanned this week: it must be found, with the right client. The morning report ends with a 'Search index' line (cases updated, documents in all); 'couldn't update' means the file or the disk needs a look.
To rebuild by hand: delete data/index.db; the next search in the review app builds it again (or, from src/, python -c "import index; index.rebuild_all('../data/clients')").

The file holds the text of every client document (Social Security numbers cut to the last four digits): keep it with the client files, under the same access and backups. Nothing is lost if it is deleted.
items.firm_what: Search across every client's documents: kept up to date every night
firm_steps: Once a quarter, search for a word from a document scanned this week. It should be found, under the right client.
If search looks out of date, the nightly run brings it up to date. If it is still wrong after a night, ask {provider} to rebuild it.
The search file holds the words of every client document: it stays on the same machine as the client files, with the same access and the same backups.
